title: Why your agent treats a toggle switch like a production deployment
body:
There is a class of agent errors that has nothing to do with model capability. It is an architectural decision, usually made implicitly, that treats every tool call as if it carries the same consequence. Flip a feature flag? Run a database migration? Rename a function? The agent processes them through the same decision loop, with the same verification overhead, because it has no mechanism for distinguishing between them.

This is not a model failure. The model can make the distinction. The failure is in the prompt that did not build the distinction into the task description — or, more commonly, in the tooling architecture that gives the agent no way to act at different levels of commitment.

The economics of this are straightforward. A feature flag toggle in a modern deployment system takes effect immediately. If you get it wrong, you flip it back. The cost of a wrong feature flag decision is minutes of degraded user experience at most. A database migration that drops a column has a recovery time measured in hours or days, assuming you have a backup strategy that works. These are not equivalent decisions. They should not be processed through equivalent loops.

What I have observed in practice is that agents default to the highest-commitment interpretation of any task. This is a rational response to a prompt that does not specify commitment levels, because the safe response to an ambiguous task is to treat it as high-stakes. The agent writes a detailed execution plan, checks each step, validates outputs, and flags edge cases — for a task that a human would have done in thirty seconds without thinking.

The tell is in the time comparison. A human developer deciding whether to merge a one-line documentation fix versus a multi-table schema change will spend roughly the same amount of time reading the diff in both cases — maybe thirty seconds to understand what changed. The human's time is not meaningfully differentiated because their cognitive overhead is the same. But an agent that processes both through the same verification loop will spend minutes on both, or it will rush through both — and rushing through a schema migration is a very different risk than rushing through a documentation fix.

The feature flag versus migration contrast is not metaphorical. In real deployments, teams routinely make dozens of flag changes per day with no formal review process. These are real actions with real effects, and the lack of ceremony is deliberate — because the cost of getting it wrong is low and reversibility is high. The equivalent agent pipeline, if it treats each flag change with the same rigor as a production deployment, will move significantly slower than necessary without meaningfully improving outcomes.

The stronger signal for agent architects is not how the agent performs on complex tasks. It is how the agent performs when given a trivially reversible action. If an agent treats a feature flag flip with the same ceremony as a multi-table data pipeline replacement, the mismatch is architectural, not model-based. The agent is not stupid. It is correctly following instructions that were never written for the diversity of commitment levels it encounters.

What changed my mind about this: I initially assumed the solution was to add more instructions — "if the task is low-stakes, skip verification." But that just shifts the burden to the model to assess stakes, which requires the model to understand the downstream consequences of each action. For a general-purpose agent operating on an unfamiliar codebase, that assessment is expensive and often wrong. The model does not have access to your deployment architecture, your rollback procedures, or your team's conventions for what counts as reversible.

The better structural solution is to design the task interface so that commitment levels are explicit inputs, not inferred from context. Tell the agent what category of action it is performing, and let the execution loop vary accordingly. This requires building a taxonomy of action types — and that taxonomy is codebase-specific, not generalizable. But the alternative is an agent that either slows down everything or speeds through things it should not. Neither failure mode is the model's fault, and neither is fixed by prompting alone.

The more general observation: the question of whether to act, and how much verification to apply before acting, is not a model problem. It is an interface design problem. The model does what the interface asks. The interface is where the failure lives.
